title: Gauss's law
examples: What is the difference between electric field and electric flux?
When can I use Gauss's law in electrostatics?
How does the shape of the Gaussian surface affect the result?

explain.say: Today we explore gauss's law in electricity.

items: Flux measures electric field passing through area
Gauss's law relates flux to enclosed charge
\epsilon0 is the permittivity of free space

explain.say: Electric flux measures the flow of electric field lines.
A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface.
Gauss's law states flux equals enclosed charge over $\epsilon0$.
Consider a sphere with charge inside, the flux is constant.
For a uniformly charged sphere, the field is like a point charge.

faq.q: Does the shape of the Gaussian surface matter for the calculation?
faq.a: No, the total electric flux only depends on the total charge enclosed. You can use any closed surface.
asks: Does the surface shape change the flux value?
Is the surface shape irrelevant for gauss's law?

faq.a: $Q{enc}$ is the total net electric charge completely enclosed within your chosen Gaussian surface. You must calculate this sum.
asks: How do I find the enclosed charge?

faq.q: Is gauss's law always the easiest method to use?
faq.a: It is easiest when the charge distribution has high symmetry, like spheres or infinite planes. Otherwise, other methods are better.
asks: When should I use gauss's law?
Does symmetry make gauss's law always best?

faq.q: What is the relationship between flux and the electric field?
faq.a: Flux is the integral of the electric field dotted with the area vector over the surface. It measures the net flow.

faq.q: Can I use gauss's law if the charge is not uniform?
faq.a: Yes, you can, as long as you can accurately calculate the total net charge enclosed within the surface. The law holds true always.
asks: Does charge uniformity matter for gauss's law?
Can gauss's law handle non-uniform charges?

facts: Electric flux ($\PhiE$) is a measure of the total electric field passing through a surface.
Gauss's law mathematically relates this flux to the net charge enclosed ($Q{enc}$).
The constant $\epsilon0$ is the permittivity of free space, approximately $8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2 \text{ N}^{-1} \text{ m}^{-2}$.
For a spherically symmetric charge, the electric field outside is the same as if all charge were at the center.

quiz.say: If the net charge inside a closed box is zero, what is the total electric flux through the box?

options.show: The flux is proportional to the box's surface area.
options.say: The flux is proportional to the box's surface area.

options.show: The flux is equal to the box's volume.
options.say: The flux is equal to the box's volume.

options.show: The flux is determined by the box's material.
options.say: The flux is determined by the box's material.

quiz.why: Gauss's law states that if the enclosed charge is zero, the net flux must also be zero.

wrong.0: While area is involved, the net flux depends only on the charge.
wrong.2: This confuses volume with electric charge or flux.
wrong.3: The flux depends only on the charge inside, not the box itself.

quiz.say: A point charge $Q$ is placed at the center of a sphere. If you double the charge, what happens to the flux through the sphere?

options.show: It increases by the square of the charge.
options.say: It increases by the square of the charge.

options.show: It remains the same because the surface is large.
options.say: It remains the same because the surface is large.

options.show: It halves because the field spreads out.
options.say: It halves because the field spreads out.

quiz.why: Since flux is directly proportional to the enclosed charge, doubling the charge doubles the flux.

wrong.1: The relationship is linear, not squared.
wrong.2: The size of the surface does not change the total flux if the charge changes.
wrong.3: While the field spreads, the total net flux scales directly with the charge.

quiz.say: If you use a cube as your Gaussian surface around a charge $Q$, the flux is:

options.show: Zero, because the cube has corners.
options.say: Zero, because the cube has corners.

options.show: Proportional to the cube's side length cubed.
options.say: Proportional to the cube's side length cubed.

options.show: Depends on the cube's orientation in space.
options.say: Depends on the cube's orientation in space.

quiz.why: Gauss's law dictates that the flux depends only on the enclosed charge $Q$, regardless of the cube's shape.

wrong.1: The corners do not affect the total net flux through a closed surface.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses volume instead of the charge relationship.
wrong.3: The total flux through a closed surface is independent of its orientation.
